title: Linux quick ops: local enumeration, privilege escalation, persistence and one-liners
intro: A grab-bag reference for working a Linux foothold: enumerate the host and your own context, hunt the usual local privilege-escalation paths (SUID/SGID, sudo rules, capabilities, cron, PATH), establish persistence, and keep the handy one-liners close. Open any node for what it means and the commands behind it. Everything here is for systems you are authorised to test: enumeration is quiet, but privilege escalation and persistence change the host and are logged, so stay inside scope and keep notes.

phases.name: Local enumeration
phases.blurb: Learn who you are, what you can run, and what the host exposes before touching anything. All read-only, all as a standard user.

nodes.label: Your context (id / sudo -l)
nodes.detail: id prints your UID, GID and groups: membership of sudo, wheel, docker, lxd, adm or disk is a lead in itself (docker and lxd group members can trivially become root). sudo -l lists what you may run through sudo and as whom, the single most valuable privesc check, because a single misconfigured rule (NOPASSWD on an abusable binary) is often the whole path. hostnamectl and uname -a give the kernel and distro.

nodes.label: Users & home dirs
nodes.detail: /etc/passwd lists every account, its shell and home directory; a world-readable /etc/shadow is an instant win (crack the hashes). Comb the home directories and /tmp, /var and web roots for keys, config and history files. The dot-files (.bash_history, .ssh, .aws, .config) are where credentials hide.

nodes.label: Network (ss / ip)
nodes.detail: ss -tulpn (or netstat -tulpn) lists listening sockets with the owning process: services bound to 127.0.0.1 are reachable only from the host, prime pivot targets. ip a and ip route map the interfaces and routes; arp -a and /etc/hosts name neighbours. A service on localhost that runs as root is often the easiest escalation on the box.

nodes.label: Processes & software
nodes.detail: ps aux shows every process and its owner, revealing root-owned services and any credential passed on a command line. Note the installed package versions (dpkg -l / rpm -qa) and the service list for known-vulnerable software. pspy (no root needed) watches processes and cron jobs over time to catch short-lived root tasks you would otherwise miss.

nodes.label: Scheduled jobs (cron)
nodes.detail: List your own crontab and read the system ones: /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d and the cron.daily/hourly directories. A root cron job that runs a script you can write to, or uses a relative path or a wildcard, is a direct escalation. If you cannot read a job, pspy will show it executing.

nodes.label: Automated scanners
nodes.detail: linPEAS is the broad enumerator: it checks SUID/SGID, sudo, capabilities, cron, writable files, kernel version and known exploits, colour-coding the likely wins. LinEnum and linux-smart-enumeration (lse.sh) cover the same ground more quietly. Run one for breadth, then verify each flagged path by hand, the scanner suggests, you confirm.

phases.name: Privilege escalation
phases.blurb: From a standard user to root. Walk the common paths in roughly decreasing order of reliability: sudo rules, SUID/SGID, capabilities, writable cron, PATH abuse, then a kernel exploit as a last resort.

nodes.label: Sudo rules + GTFOBins
nodes.detail: sudo -l is where most Linux escalations start. Any binary you may run as root through sudo is a candidate: look it up on GTFOBins for the 'sudo' escape that spawns a shell or reads a protected file. Even seemingly harmless tools (find, vim, less, awk, tar, env, python) have a documented escape. Watch for NOPASSWD entries and for env_keep settings (LD_PRELOAD / LD_LIBRARY_PATH with SETENV let you load a malicious library as root).

children.label: Sudo version CVEs
children.detail: The sudo binary itself has had serious bugs: Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156), a heap overflow exploitable by any local user regardless of sudoers, and the 2023 chroot flaw (CVE-2025-32463 on recent versions). Check the version against known CVEs before assuming you need a sudoers rule at all.

nodes.label: SUID / SGID binaries
nodes.detail: A SUID binary runs with the file owner's privileges (root), whoever executes it, so an abusable root-owned SUID is a shell. Find them with find and the -perm mask, then check each against GTFOBins for the 'SUID' entry. Custom or unusual SUID binaries are the most promising: a company-built helper rarely drops privileges correctly. SGID (-2000) is the group equivalent.

children.label: GTFOBins SUID escapes
children.detail: The common wins, each on GTFOBins: a SUID find runs find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; (the -p keeps the elevated privileges), a SUID bash needs bash -p, and nmap, vim, less, cp, env and dozens more have documented SUID escapes. The GTFOBins reference examples are in the table below. If a binary is not a known one, search its name plus 'SUID privilege escalation'.

nodes.label: Capabilities (getcap)
nodes.detail: Linux capabilities split root's power into units a binary can hold without being full SUID. getcap -r / lists every file with capabilities. cap_setuid+ep on an interpreter (python, perl, ruby) is as good as root: the program can set its UID to 0 itself. cap_dac_read_search reads any file; cap_dac_override writes any file. Check each capability against GTFOBins' 'Capabilities' entry.

nodes.label: Writable cron / scripts
nodes.detail: A root cron job that executes a script you can write to runs your code as root on its next tick. Find world-writable files and directories, cross-reference with the cron jobs, and look for jobs that call a script by a relative path or expand a wildcard (tar/rsync wildcard injection). Append a reverse shell or a chmod +s /bin/bash to the script and wait for the schedule.

nodes.label: PATH abuse
nodes.detail: When a root-run script or SUID binary calls another program by name instead of an absolute path (service, cat, ps), the shell resolves it through PATH. If you can prepend a directory you control to PATH, your malicious binary of that name runs as root. Classic against a SUID wrapper that shells out: create a fake 'service' in /tmp, put /tmp first in PATH, run the wrapper.
cmd: cd /tmp; echo '/bin/bash -p' > service; chmod +x service; export PATH=/tmp:$PATH

nodes.label: Kernel & exploit suggesters
nodes.detail: If configuration yields nothing, the kernel version may. linux-exploit-suggester (les.sh) and linux-exploit-suggester-2 compare uname -a against a database of kernel CVEs and rank candidates (DirtyCow, DirtyPipe, OverlayFS, pwnkit). Kernel exploits can panic the host, so treat them as a last resort and prefer a stable, well-documented one on an authorised test.

children.label: pwnkit / DirtyPipe
children.detail: Two near-universal local roots worth knowing: pwnkit (CVE-2021-4034) abuses pkexec's argument handling and hits almost every distro from 2009 onward; DirtyPipe (CVE-2022-0847) overwrites read-only files via a pipe-buffer flaw on kernels 5.8 to 5.16.11. Both have reliable public exploits; confirm the pkexec version and kernel before running.

phases.name: Persistence
phases.blurb: Survive a reboot or a dropped session. On an authorised test, record every mechanism you add so it can be removed in the clean-up.

nodes.label: SSH authorized_keys
nodes.detail: The quietest foothold: append your public key to a user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and you can log in as them over SSH with no password, as long as the key stays. Root's authorized_keys gives passwordless root. Needs write access to the target user's .ssh (you already have it for your own user). Remove the line during clean-up.

nodes.label: Cron job
nodes.detail: A cron entry re-launches a reverse shell on a schedule. A user crontab (crontab -e) needs no root and fires as that user; a line in /etc/cron.d or a root crontab fires as root. Keep the interval modest and the command plausible. List and remove with the same tool.

nodes.label: systemd unit / timer
nodes.detail: A systemd service that restarts on failure, or a timer, is durable persistence. A unit in /etc/systemd/system runs as root (needs root to write); a user unit under ~/.config/systemd/user runs as you with lingering enabled. Enable it so it starts at boot. More robust than cron but more visible to an admin reviewing units.

nodes.label: Shell startup files
nodes.detail: A line in ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile or /etc/profile.d/ runs every time that user opens a shell, no scheduler needed. Useful to re-trigger a payload on the next interactive login. Quiet, but only fires on login, so pair it with another mechanism. Record the exact line you added.

phases.name: Handy one-liners
phases.blurb: The commands you reach for again and again: spawning a proper shell, transferring files, and upgrading a dumb shell to an interactive one.

nodes.label: Upgrade to a TTY
nodes.detail: A raw reverse shell has no job control, no tab completion and dies on Ctrl-C. Upgrade it: spawn a PTY with Python, then background it and set the terminal to raw so you get a full interactive shell with history and arrow keys. The stty rows/cols step makes full-screen tools (vim, less) render correctly.

nodes.label: Reverse shells
nodes.detail: When you have command execution and want a shell back. bash /dev/tcp is built in and needs nothing extra; nc with -e (or the mkfifo variant where -e is stripped) and a Python one-liner cover the rest. Start a listener (nc -lvnp 443) on your host first. The attacker IP here is a placeholder.

nodes.label: File transfer
nodes.detail: Move tooling onto the box or loot off it. Serve a directory from your host with Python's HTTP server, then pull with wget or curl. scp works when you have SSH. For a quick paste, base64 the file and decode it on the far side. The host here is the attacker's HTTP server.
cmd: base64 -w0 file | xclip  # then: echo <b64> | base64 -d > file

nodes.label: Find interesting files
nodes.detail: Sweep the filesystem for the things that matter: world-writable files and directories, files owned by root that you can write, recently modified files, and credentials in config. Redirect stderr to /dev/null to cut the permission-denied noise.

references.title: Linux capabilities worth hunting
references.intro: What each capability grants when set on a binary via getcap. cap_setuid is the clearest win. Filter by capability.
rows: The binary can set its UID to 0: on an interpreter (python/perl), instant root
Bypass read permission checks: read any file, including /etc/shadow
Bypass all file permission checks: write any file
Broad admin operations (mount, namespaces); many abuse paths
Attach to and inject into any process, including root processes
Change file ownership; chain to take over a root-owned file
